task.goal: Create a low-pressure public poetry activity in a covered market that invites people to combine ordinary words they overhear without recording anyone's speech.
hard_constraints: No audio recording, quotation attributed to a person, or solicitation from shoppers.
Use only a freestanding paper board for one afternoon; do not mark the building or block stalls.
Participation and display must be optional, and volunteers remove the board at closing.
task.available_resources: Paper cards, pencils, freestanding board and two volunteers.
task.expected_result: Several distinct creative formats and a small way to observe participation and comfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Word Exchange
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
A shared word bank lets strangers combine ordinary vocabulary without preserving anyone’s conversation. A passive invitation on the freestanding paper board reads: “If you wish, remember one ordinary word you happen to hear. Write only that word—no names, speakers, or phrases. Combine it with two words already here to make a tiny poem.” Volunteers seed the bank with common words such as “bag,” “later,” and “green,” explicitly marked as starter words.

Participants may add a word, write a poem, or simply look. They can keep their card, erase it, or place it in a folded paper pocket marked “Optional display.” Separate pockets hold single words and finished poems. The mechanism is exchange: vocabulary contributed independently becomes material for someone else, reducing the pressure to invent a complete poem alone.

One volunteer quietly maintains the board; the other checks that its permitted position leaves stalls and circulation clear. Neither approaches shoppers or requests contributions. Instructions exclude identifying details, sensitive words, and remembered sentences. This assumes market permission and a board that can support folded paper pockets made from the available cards. Words may repeat, and volunteers cannot verify their origin; the activity depends on clear instructions rather than surveillance. Both volunteers remove the board and all cards at closing.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate two short periods: a simple “Make a poem from ordinary words” invitation and the word-exchange instructions, keeping placement and volunteer behavior constant. Tally voluntary starts and completed poems without identifying people. Add an optional card asking, “Easy to join / unsure / felt pressured.” The exchange mechanism is unsupported if it produces no more starts or if participants repeatedly copy phrases or ask whether they must contribute. A small afternoon sample can expose problems, not establish effectiveness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A Walk Through Words
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Turn the board into a branching poem map. Draw three loose columns on its paper surface: “something,” “doing,” and “somewhere or somehow.” Seed each with a few ordinary starter words. A passive sign invites visitors to add one ordinary word they happen to overhear, without retaining a phrase, speaker, name, or identifying detail. Nobody is approached.

Visitors make a poem by choosing one word from each column and reading a route across the board. They may rearrange the order, add small connecting words, or write their route on a card. Reading silently counts as full participation; writing and display are explicitly optional. Cards can be kept or placed in a folded paper display pocket.

The mechanism is spatial composition: the board supplies a visible structure that turns choosing into writing. Unlike exchanging completed contributions, the same word field supports many private poems, so someone can participate without leaving a trace. The columns offer a starting point, although unusual words need not fit neatly and grammatical categories could feel restrictive. Include “Any order is welcome” prominently.

With market permission, one volunteer keeps the freestanding board clear of stall access while the other maintains legibility and space for additions. Only its paper surface is marked. The layout assumes enough readable board area and may work poorly where people cannot pause comfortably. Volunteers remove everything at closing.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype two small sections on the same board: an unstructured cluster of starter words and a three-column map using identical words. Invite visitors through the written instructions to use either section; alternate their positions halfway through. Count voluntarily displayed poems by section and offer an optional “clear / confusing / too restrictive” response card. If the map yields no visible use, or repeated confusion about valid routes, its structure needs simplifying. Private reading remains unmeasured; do not treat a lack of displayed cards as proof of nonparticipation.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One Word Changes the Weather
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Offer poetry as a tiny act of revision. Write several short, clearly labeled volunteer-made starter lines on the paper board, such as “The basket carries the morning” and “Today waits beside the door.” A passive invitation says: “If you wish, replace one word with an ordinary word you happen to overhear. Change one more word if you like. Keep the result or choose to display it.” Include a clear rule against remembered phrases, names, speaker descriptions, or attribution.

Participants copy a starter onto a card and substitute their word. They can stop after one change, rewrite further, or leave without displaying anything. A folded paper pocket holds optional finished versions alongside their starter labels. Nobody changes another participant’s card. This produces families of related poems whose differences are easy to notice.

The mechanism is semantic surprise through substitution: a familiar sentence supplies rhythm and a low-effort starting point, while one displaced word can change its mood or meaning. It assumes the starter lines are accessible and inviting. Their vocabulary and tone will influence every result, and some participants may find the exercise too constrained; permission to rewrite further offers an exit without requiring originality.

Two volunteers install the freestanding board in a market-approved position away from stalls and circulation, maintain readable instructions, and answer only when approached. No recording or shopper solicitation occurs. Only the board’s paper is marked, and all materials leave with the volunteers at closing.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Place two matched starter lines on the board: one with the substitution instruction and one with “Use this line as inspiration for a poem.” Alternate which line receives which instruction halfway through. Count optional displayed responses and inspect whether substitutions create noticeably different meanings rather than merely copying the starter. Provide an optional “easy / limiting / uncomfortable” response card. If substitution produces mostly unchanged copies or repeated “limiting” feedback, its promised low-pressure entry may be coming at too great a creative cost. Counts cannot reveal the comfort of silent visitors.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A Poem for the Mouth
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make sound, rather than sentence meaning, the starting point. A passive invitation on the freestanding paper board reads: “If you wish, notice two ordinary words you happen to overhear separately. Keep only isolated words, never a phrase or who said it. Can their sounds make a tiny poem?” Volunteer-made examples, clearly labeled as invented, demonstrate repetition, rhyme, and contrasting sounds.

Participants write their two words on a card, then repeat, stretch, or connect them with words of their own. “Small / stall,” for example, might become “small rain / tall stall / small rain.” Rhyming is optional; an awkward sound can be useful. Silent reading counts, and nobody is asked to perform aloud. Participants can keep their cards or voluntarily copy a poem onto the board’s paper surface.

The mechanism is attention to rhythm and sound: ordinary vocabulary becomes material through how words meet in the mouth. This could help people who feel they need an important message before writing poetry. Unlike a word bank or sentence template, it supplies a listening lens rather than shared content or syntax.

With market permission, two volunteers place the board clear of stalls and circulation. Cards and pencils sit in folded paper holders supported by the board; this requires a board that can accommodate them. Volunteers answer questions only when approached and remove everything at closing. Instructions exclude names, identifying details, sensitive content, and remembered sentences. There is no audio recording, attribution, or solicitation. Sound play may be less accessible across languages or for some visitors; invented connecting words and silent composition remain welcome.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Give equal board space to the sound prompt and a simple comparator: “Combine two isolated ordinary words you overhear into a tiny poem.” Use the same privacy and optional-display instructions for both. Participants may optionally mark their chosen prompt and “easy / confusing / uncomfortable” on a response card. Volunteers tally only voluntarily submitted cards. Inspect whether the sound prompt produces recognizable repetition or sound relationships and whether comments suggest pressure to rhyme or perform. Repeated confusion or greater reported discomfort would challenge its usefulness. Sparse responses cannot establish which prompt attracts more participation, and silent participation remains unknown.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Let the Cards Decide
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a small private shuffle to interrupt the search for a clever idea. The board’s passive invitation reads: “If you wish, put three ordinary words you happen to overhear separately on three cards—one word per card. No phrases, names, speaker details, or attribution. Turn them face down, mix them, then reveal them in a row. Make a tiny poem in that order, adding your own words if helpful.” No shared word bank is needed.

A participant might privately collect “tomorrow,” “paper,” and “warm.” An accidental order such as “warm / tomorrow / paper” becomes a puzzle to interpret. Participants may reshuffle once, ignore an unhelpful word, or stop. They keep their cards unless they choose to copy the finished poem onto the board. Volunteers never collect or display the source cards by default.

The mechanism is chance followed by interpretation: an arbitrary sequence supplies a creative decision that the participant does not have to justify. It could reduce the pressure to choose the best opening while producing surprising connections between unrelated words. The private shuffle distinguishes this from exchanging vocabulary or following a fixed sentence. It assumes participants can handle three cards at the board; the extra steps may instead feel cumbersome.

Two volunteers set up the freestanding paper board in a market-approved position clear of stalls and circulation. Folded paper holders keep cards and pencils on the board, assuming its construction supports them; participants hold their own shuffle. Only the board’s paper is marked. Volunteers do not approach shoppers, record speech, or request contributions. A written notice makes participation and display optional and excludes sensitive or identifying material. Both volunteers remove the board and all remaining materials at closing.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For two equal short periods, alternate the shuffle prompt with “Choose any order for your three words and make a tiny poem.” Keep placement and privacy instructions constant. An optional response card asks which version was used and whether arranging the words felt “helpful / fiddly / uncomfortable.” Count only voluntarily submitted poems and feedback. If shuffling repeatedly causes procedural questions, abandoned card handling, or “fiddly” responses, its reduction in decision pressure may not justify its effort. Time periods attract different visitors, so this is a usability check, not evidence of a causal participation increase.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Poem Left Behind
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make a poem by removing words. The board’s passive invitation reads: “If you wish, write six ordinary words you happen to overhear separately. Keep no sentences, names, identifying details, or information about speakers. Cross out words until a tiny poem remains. Add your own connecting words if useful.” Nobody needs to listen deliberately or wait to collect enough words; clearly labeled invented starter words offer an immediate starting point.

Participants work on a paper card held in their hand. They can cross out any number of words, change their mind on another card, or stop. Their cards stay private unless they choose to copy the surviving poem onto the board’s paper surface. The notice explicitly makes both participation and display optional.

The mechanism is subtraction: selecting what survives can reveal an unexpected relationship without requiring someone to compose a polished sentence. The crossed-out material also gives the participant something concrete to react to. This differs from arranging a word bank because deletion, including the gaps it leaves, creates the poem.

With market permission, two volunteers position the freestanding board outside stall access and circulation routes. Folded paper holders carry cards and pencils, assuming the board can support them. Volunteers answer questions only when approached, do not solicit shoppers, and make no audio recordings. They remove the board and remaining materials at closing.

The main limits are the effort of collecting six words and the possibility that crossing things out feels like correcting mistakes. The instructions therefore say “Nothing here is wrong; removal is just a way to choose.”
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Offer two labeled prompts with equal space and identical starter words: “Remove words until a poem remains” and “Use any of these words to write a poem.” Swap their positions halfway through the afternoon. Participants may optionally leave a feedback card identifying their prompt and marking “easy to begin / hard to begin / uncomfortable.” Count only voluntarily displayed poems and submitted feedback; do not track individuals. If deletion repeatedly needs explanation or receives more “hard to begin” responses, its proposed advantage is doubtful. A small, self-selected sample checks usability, not comparative effectiveness or the comfort of silent visitors.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Two Strangers, One Tiny Poem
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a voluntary unfinished line to give the next writer something to answer. Divide the board’s paper into a few paired spaces labeled “Opening” and “Reply.” A passive invitation says: “If you wish, make a short opening using two ordinary words you happen to overhear separately. Or answer an opening already here, using an ordinary word you happen to overhear and words of your own. Invent the connection.” Clearly labeled volunteer-written openings allow participation before visitors contribute.

Participants draft privately on cards. They may keep the result or choose to copy it into an empty opening or reply space. Posting an opening explicitly invites one invented reply; nobody edits another person’s writing. Completed pairs stay together. A participant can answer privately without displaying anything.

The mechanism is reciprocal imagination: another person’s invented line supplies an unresolved situation, and the reply changes its meaning. This could make writing feel like responding to a small gift rather than inventing a whole poem alone. For example, a volunteer-created opening might say, “The basket forgot tomorrow”; a reply could give that imaginary basket a destination. Examples and contributions must never reproduce overheard sentences or identify speakers.

Implementation needs only the freestanding paper board, cards, pencils, and two volunteers, plus permission for a position clear of stalls and circulation. Folded paper holders require a board capable of supporting them. Volunteers explain only when approached, never solicit shoppers, make no audio recordings, and remove everything at closing.

Participation and display are explicitly optional. The main uncertainty is social obligation: an unanswered opening might feel rejected, or replying might feel intrusive. The notice says, “Openings may remain unanswered; every contribution is complete enough.”
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Place a small paired-writing section beside an equally sized independent prompt: “Combine ordinary words into your own tiny poem.” Alternate their positions halfway through. Count optional displayed contributions and how many openings receive replies. Offer optional feedback: “helped me start / felt obliged to answer / preferred writing alone.” Repeated obligation feedback, or openings accumulating without replies while independent poems appear, challenges the mechanism. Inspect completed pairs for whether replies develop the opening rather than merely repeat it. These observations cannot establish how private participants felt.

EXPAND.title: Echo Pairs
EXPAND.proposal:
Make sound the invitation: “Two ordinary words can make a poem because of how they sound.” On the paper board, volunteers write invented examples such as “pear / repair” and “tin / tomorrow,” clearly labeled as examples. Visitors may privately recall two ordinary, nonidentifying words heard incidentally and pair them through rhyme, repeated consonants, or a pleasing sound. They can repeat the pair, add connecting words, or leave it as two words. No searching for speakers or deliberate listening is requested.

The mechanism is phonetic association: sound supplies a relationship even when the words seem unrelated in meaning. Unlike the prior column map, this offers a way to decide which words belong together without classifying them. It assumes visitors can find a sound connection; pronunciation differences and literacy may make the prompt harder for some people. The sign therefore accepts “any sound connection you enjoy.”

Participants may compose silently, write a card to keep, or write their poem directly in an optional display area. The sign prohibits names, identifying details, remembered phrases, and attribution; there is no audio recording. Volunteers never approach shoppers. One maintains the paper surface and answers questions initiated by visitors; the other watches clearance.

Use only the board, cards, and pencils, with market permission and a position outside stall access and circulation. If the board becomes crowded or unstable, pause the activity. Volunteers remove it and all remaining materials at closing.
EXPAND.experiment: For a first trial, the board volunteer alternates two 20-minute prompts: sound pairing and the prior three-column map, using equal space and clearly invented examples. Count optional displayed poems and requests for explanation; offer an optional “comfortable / unsure / uncomfortable” pencil response. Inspect whether sound-based poems actually use audible relationships. Stop the sound prompt after repeated confusion or any reported pressure to listen closely to strangers. No improvement is supported if it produces fewer usable poems or more confusion without a comfort benefit. Silent participation remains unknown.

EXPAND.title: Questions With Unexpected Answers
EXPAND.proposal:
Invite visitors to turn ordinary words into a miniature riddle. The board reads: “Recall two ordinary words you happened to hear separately. Make one into a question and let the other answer.” A clearly invented example is “What does a basket dream of? / Tuesday.” Visitors invent the question themselves; they do not reproduce a question heard in the market. Either word can take either role, and no sensible answer is required.

The mechanism is a deliberately unexpected semantic relationship. A question creates anticipation, and an unrelated answer changes how both words feel. Compared with the prior substitution exercise, visitors generate the relationship and wording rather than inherit a volunteer’s sentence. This could broaden expression, but it also requires more invention and may feel like a wit contest. The board explicitly welcomes plain, puzzling, or unfinished results.

Reading is welcome. Composition can stay entirely private; cards may be kept, and writing in the board’s display area is optional. Instructions allow only isolated, nonidentifying words from incidental hearing: no names, remembered phrases, speaker descriptions, attribution, or audio recording. Volunteers do not invite shoppers verbally.

With market permission, one volunteer prepares the prompt and answers visitor-initiated questions; the other keeps the freestanding board clear of stalls and walking routes. Only its paper surface is marked. If someone displays identifiable material, the board volunteer covers that entry with a blank paper card while resolving it, or closes that display area if covering cannot be secured. Both volunteers remove everything at closing. The format needs only the stated materials and enough readable board space.
EXPAND.experiment: The board volunteer runs one 20-minute question-and-answer period and one equally long substitution period, reversing their order for a second pair if time permits. Compare optional displayed poems, help requests, and optional “easy to begin / hard to begin / felt pressured” marks. Inspect whether responses establish a question–answer relationship rather than copy the example. Retire the prompt if visitors repeatedly interpret it as asking shoppers questions. It offers no demonstrated advantage if its greater writing effort reduces participation without producing more varied relationships or better reported comfort.

EXPAND.title: The Folded Surprise Duet
EXPAND.proposal:
Use concealment to let two anonymous contributors make something neither could plan alone. A passive board instruction invites a visitor to write one ordinary, nonidentifying word they happened to overhear on the upper half of a card, fold that half inward, and leave the card in a labeled folded-paper holder. A second willing visitor takes a folded card, writes their own incidental word on the exposed half without opening it, then unfolds it. They may invent a connecting line, keep the result, or copy it into the optional board display.

The mechanism is independent contribution followed by revelation. Unlike the prior open word exchange, the second contributor cannot select a compatible first word; the surprise creates the compositional problem. This can distribute authorship and reduce the need to originate a whole poem, although handling steps and unpredictable waiting add friction.

Both contribution and pickup are optional. The sign states that deposited cards are offered for another visitor to complete and keep. Volunteers seed several cards with clearly marked invented words so the activity works before anyone contributes. If the holder empties, visitors can make both halves themselves or use another marked starter; nobody is recruited to replenish it.

Assume the board can support a holder folded from the available paper cards within its footprint; otherwise do not use this format. Instructions prohibit recorded speech, remembered phrases, identifying material, and attribution. Volunteers never solicit shoppers. One manages the holder and visitor-initiated questions; the other protects clearance in the market-approved location. Pause if cards spill or handling creates congestion. Volunteers remove the board and all unclaimed cards at closing.
EXPAND.experiment: The holder volunteer owns a 30-minute prototype followed by a matched open-exchange period. Count completed optional displays, abandoned folded cards, and requests for procedural help; invite an optional comfort mark. Inspect whether revealed pairs inspire connecting lines. Stop immediately if cards spread beyond the board footprint, and retire the format if repeated help is needed. Concealment has not improved the activity if surprise yields no additional creative variation while completion drops or handling burden rises. Deposited cards alone do not count as completed poems.

EXPAND.title: Words That Take a Shape
EXPAND.proposal:
Invite visitors to make a tiny visual poem from two ordinary words they happen to overhear separately. The board offers three actions: repeat a word, change its size, or place space between words. A clearly invented example shows “rain” descending toward a single “roof.” Visitors choose their own relationship: one word might surround another, drift away from it, or form a small pile. Artistic drawing is unnecessary.

The mechanism is expressive typography: position and repetition carry meaning that a sentence would otherwise have to explain. Unlike the prior branching map, the layout is the resulting poem, rather than a route for selecting words. This may help people who enjoy arranging marks more than writing sentences. It also demands more paper space and may disadvantage visitors who find small writing or visual composition difficult; a two-word horizontal arrangement is explicitly accepted.

People can imagine a layout, make a card to keep, or draw directly in a bounded optional display area. They need not submit or show a card. Instructions request isolated, nonidentifying words from incidental hearing and prohibit names, remembered phrases, speaker descriptions, attribution, and audio recording. Neither volunteer approaches shoppers.

With market permission, one volunteer draws a few generous display boxes on the board’s paper and answers questions only when approached. The other maintains clear access to stalls and circulation. Use pencils and cards only; there is no attachment requirement. When display boxes fill, visitors can continue privately on cards, and volunteers explain that limit on the board. Pause if people cluster into the walking route. Both volunteers remove the board and remaining materials at closing.
EXPAND.experiment: The board volunteer compares a 20-minute visual-poem period with a 20-minute plain two-word-poem period, each with the same display area. Count optional contributions, space used per contribution, and help requests. Offer optional “comfortable / unsure / uncomfortable” marks. Inspect whether placement changes the words’ relationship; decorative handwriting alone is insufficient evidence for the mechanism. Stop display participation if clearance is affected. Prefer the simple comparator if visual poems consume substantially more space or create more hesitation without producing meaningful spatial relationships. Private compositions cannot be assessed from the board.

EXPAND.title: A Walk Through Words, With a Clear Display Handoff
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “A Walk Through Words.” Keep its three-column word map, labeled invented starter words, flexible reading order, and optional private composition. The changed action is that visitors offer additions on cards rather than writing directly on the public board. This closes a privacy gap: instructions alone cannot prevent a remembered sentence or identifying detail from becoming public immediately.

The passive invitation reads: “If you wish, offer one ordinary word you happened to hear. No names, phrases, or details about a speaker. Choose words from the map to make a tiny poem, in any order. Reading silently counts.” Participants may keep their cards. Display requires a separate pencil mark giving permission.

One volunteer owns acceptance and copies only permitted, nonidentifying contributions onto the board’s paper. Before acceptance, the visitor retains the card; there is no submission queue. If the volunteer is interrupted or uncertain about an entry, the card stays private and the visitor can use existing words. The second volunteer maintains clearance. If an unsuitable entry reaches the board, suspend public display until it can be fully obscured; otherwise end display and continue private card composition.

The mechanism remains spatial selection. Compared with the original map, screening reduces immediate disclosure risk but adds copying work and waiting. Keep the bank small and stop accepting additions when copying would create a queue. This requires market permission, a stable board with adequate paper space, cards, pencils, and two volunteers. No attachments are needed. Nobody approaches shoppers, records speech, or attributes quotations. Participation and display are optional; volunteers remove everything at closing.
EXPAND.experiment: The board volunteer runs a 25-minute prototype with a small seeded map. Tally accepted additions, optional displayed poems, requests for explanation, and occasions when copying would require a queue. Offer optional “comfortable / unsure / uncomfortable” marks on cards, with no identifying information. Inspect whether displayed poems combine words and whether the acceptance step is understood. Pause additions as soon as waiting obstructs circulation; fall back to the existing bank and private cards. Compared with direct board writing, the expected tradeoff is fewer unchecked disclosures for more volunteer work; this trial can reveal friction but cannot establish a comfort improvement or measure silent participation.

EXPAND.title: Two Changes, One New Weather
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “One Word Changes the Weather.” Preserve volunteer-made starter lines and semantic surprise through substitution, but change the core instruction from one replacement to two replacements using separate ordinary words heard incidentally. The original can produce a poem with only one overheard word; this change makes combining overheard words part of the working procedure.

The board offers clearly invented lines with two replaceable positions, such as “The [basket] carries the [morning].” Its passive invitation says: “Recall two ordinary words you happened to hear separately. Put them into a starter line. Change the grammar or rewrite further if you wish.” Exclude remembered phrases, names, identifying details, speaker descriptions, and attribution. Do not ask anyone to listen for more material. Someone who recalls only one word may use an explicitly labeled invented starter word or simply read; that fallback supports participation but does not demonstrate combining two overheard words.

Participants compose privately on cards, keep them, or voluntarily copy a finished line into a bounded display area on the board’s paper. No attachments are necessary. Compared with the source, the second substitution can create a stronger collision of meanings, but raises recall and writing demands. The board volunteer owns simplification: if visitors repeatedly stall over finding two words, switch the written prompt to the one-word fallback for the rest of the afternoon.

Assume market permission and a stable position clear of stalls and walking routes. One volunteer maintains the prompt and answers only visitor-initiated questions; the other maintains clearance. No shopper solicitation or audio recording occurs. Writing and display are optional. Volunteers remove the board and remaining materials at closing.
EXPAND.experiment: The board volunteer tries the two-word prompt for 20 minutes, followed by a 20-minute version of the source’s one-word prompt using comparable starter lines. Tally optional displayed poems and help requests; invite optional marks for “easy to begin / hard to begin / felt pressured.” Inspect whether two replacements create a new relationship and whether participants voluntarily indicate using two recalled words or the starter-word fallback. Do not verify words against anyone’s speech. Switch early to the fallback after three separate requests for help recalling a second word, or immediately if anyone reports feeling encouraged to monitor strangers. The small comparison can expose added burden and creative possibilities; order effects and private participation remain uncertain.

EXPAND.title: The Poem You Leave Behind
EXPAND.proposal:
Use subtraction as the creative mechanism. Instead of choosing a relationship and then building a poem, visitors make an untidy pool of ordinary words and discover a poem by crossing words out. The passive board prompt reads: “If a few ordinary words you happened to hear come to mind, write them separately in a mixed-up order. Cross out any you do not need. Let the two or more words left become a poem. No sentence required.”

A clearly invented example shows “bag / blue / later / door / almost” reduced to “blue / almost.” Visitors may change the surviving words’ order. They must not reconstruct a conversation: use isolated, nonidentifying words, with no remembered phrases, names, speaker details, or attribution. If only two words come to mind, start with those and optionally add labeled invented starter words before subtracting. Nobody is asked to gather words or approach shoppers.

The distinct working principle is reduction: permission to discard material replaces the demand to invent connecting language. This removes a step shared by several earlier formats. Compared with a simple two-word poem, it offers a concrete editing action, but requires more pencil work and may make some visitors feel their first choices were wrong. The sign explicitly permits keeping every word or stopping unfinished.

Participants work on cards they can keep. Display is optional: they may copy only the surviving words into a bounded area of the board’s paper. One volunteer maintains the prompt and answers questions initiated by visitors; the other maintains clearance. With market permission, use a stable freestanding board away from stalls, cards, and pencils only. No audio recording occurs.
